walkthroughs.title: Fever, cough and pain on deep breathing

doorway: I have had fever and a bad cough, and now it hurts when I breathe deeply.
Vital signs are available on the chart.
Perform a focused history and physical examination, discuss your plan, and document only what you obtain.

plan.notice: Read temperature, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation together; fever alone does not establish pneumonia.
plan.pivot: Clarify onset, sputum, breathlessness and pleuritic pain. Ask hemoptysis and thromboembolic risks rather than assuming every cough is infectious.
plan.exam: Compare equivalent posterior lung sites, then percussion and tactile findings where the case supports them. Document the location of a focal abnormality.
plan.avoid: Writing both lungs clear after listening at one site, or omitting oxygen saturation from the supplied vitals.

goals: Use focal lung findings to localize the problem.
Sputum color alone does not establish a bacterial cause.
Assess severity before deciding outpatient follow-up.
walkthroughs.variant_guidance: Use this core presentation to learn the sequence before transferring to a variation.

timeline.student: Hello, I am a medical student. I will listen to your concerns, examine you with your permission, and discuss the next steps.
timeline.patient: Hello. Thank you for introducing yourself. I am ready to talk.

timeline.student: What brings you in today?
timeline.patient: I have had fever and a bad cough, and now it hurts when I breathe deeply.
timeline.why: Read temperature, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation together; fever alone does not establish pneumonia.

timeline.student: When did your symptoms first begin?
timeline.patient: The cough began 4 days ago.
timeline.why: Clarify onset, sputum, breathlessness and pleuritic pain. Ask hemoptysis and thromboembolic risks rather than assuming every cough is infectious.

timeline.student: How have the cough and fever changed since they began?
timeline.patient: The fever began the next day and the cough is getting worse.
timeline.why: Change over time can change urgency even when the symptom is familiar.

timeline.student: Where do you feel the symptoms?
timeline.patient: The discomfort is in my right lower chest.

timeline.student: Does the discomfort spread anywhere else?
timeline.patient: The pain stays there.
timeline.why: Spread of discomfort can connect an apparent local complaint with another system.

timeline.student: What does it feel like?
timeline.patient: It is a sharp pain when I cough or breathe deeply.
timeline.why: Use the patient’s words before translating them into a clinical description.

timeline.student: How bad are the symptoms, and how do they affect what you can do?
timeline.patient: The pain is 5/10.
timeline.why: Intensity and functional effect are distinct; record only the dimension answered.

timeline.student: Have you been around anyone who was ill?
timeline.patient: My coworker had a respiratory illness last week.

timeline.student: What makes it better?
timeline.patient: Acetaminophen lowers the fever for a few hours.
timeline.why: Relief changes probability, but is not proof that a serious cause is excluded.

timeline.student: What makes it worse?
timeline.patient: Coughing and deep breathing worsen the pain.
timeline.why: Compare triggers with the chronology; one trigger does not establish a diagnosis.

timeline.student: What have you tried for this, and did it help?
timeline.patient: I took acetaminophen 500 mg twice yesterday.

timeline.student: Have you had anything like this before?
timeline.patient: I have not had an episode like this before.

timeline.student: Have you had a cough?
timeline.patient: I cough up yellow sputum.
timeline.why: Use this answer to weigh the possibilities described in the reasoning section.

timeline.student: Have you felt short of breath?
timeline.patient: I am short of breath on stairs.
timeline.why: Use this answer to weigh the possibilities described in the reasoning section.

timeline.student: Have you had a fever?
timeline.patient: I measured 101.5 at home.
timeline.why: Use this answer to weigh the possibilities described in the reasoning section.

timeline.student: Have you had chills?
timeline.patient: I had shaking chills last night.
timeline.why: Use this answer to weigh the possibilities described in the reasoning section.

timeline.student: Have you felt unusually tired or low in energy?
timeline.patient: I feel wiped out.
timeline.why: Use this answer to weigh the possibilities described in the reasoning section.

timeline.student: Have you had any chest pain?
timeline.patient: The right chest pain is worse with a deep breath.
timeline.why: Use this answer to weigh the possibilities described in the reasoning section.

timeline.student: Have you coughed up any blood?
timeline.patient: No blood in the sputum.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: Have you noticed swelling in your legs or ankles?
timeline.patient: Neither leg is swollen.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: Have you actually passed out or lost consciousness?
timeline.patient: I have not fainted.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: What medical conditions have you been diagnosed with?
timeline.patient: No chronic lung or heart disease, vaccines not reviewed recently.

timeline.student: Have you had any surgeries or hospital admissions?
timeline.patient: Hernia repair at age 20.

timeline.student: Have you had recent surgery?
timeline.patient: I have not had recent surgery.

timeline.student: What medicines do you take, including prescriptions, over-the-counter products, and supplements?
timeline.patient: I took acetaminophen. I do not take daily prescription medications.
timeline.why: Name, dose and frequency matter; do not fill in missing details.

timeline.student: Do you have any medication allergies, and what reaction do you have?
timeline.patient: No known drug allergies.
timeline.why: Distinguish the substance and reaction from a blanket allergy label.

timeline.student: Do you use tobacco or smoke?
timeline.patient: Smokes 5 cigarettes daily for 5 years.

timeline.student: Do you drink alcohol, and how much?
timeline.patient: Two alcoholic drinks weekly.

timeline.student: Do you use any recreational drugs?
timeline.patient: No recreational drugs.

timeline.student: What do you do for work?
timeline.patient: I am a bus dispatcher.

timeline.student: Who do you live with?
timeline.patient: I live with my wife.

timeline.student: Have you traveled recently?
timeline.patient: I have not traveled recently.

timeline.student: Have you recently been immobilized or on bed rest?
timeline.patient: I have not been immobilized recently.

timeline.student: What health problems has your mother had?
timeline.patient: My mother is fifty-two and she has asthma.
timeline.why: Record which relative and the condition; do not infer a family history from patient worry.

timeline.student: What health problems has your father had?
timeline.patient: My father is fifty-five and he has high blood pressure.
timeline.why: Record which relative and the condition; do not infer a family history from patient worry.

timeline.student: What health problems have your siblings had?
timeline.patient: I have one sister, she's twenty-seven and she's healthy.
timeline.why: Record which relative and the condition; do not infer a family history from patient worry.

timeline.student: What worries you most about these symptoms?
timeline.patient: Could I give this to the people at home?
timeline.why: FIFE helps connect the clinical plan with this patient’s concern and circumstances.

timeline.student: Thank you for explaining that. I can understand why this is concerning.
timeline.patient: As I mentioned, could I give this to the people at home?

timeline.student: May I have your permission to examine you?
timeline.patient: Yes, that's fine. Go ahead.

timeline.action: Clean hands, provide privacy and appropriate draping, explain the selected examination and help the patient into a comfortable position.
timeline.why: These are stated actions in this written example. A visual avatar does not verify hand hygiene, consent or hands-on technique.

timeline.action: General appearance
timeline.finding: Tired appearing, alert and oriented, speaking full sentences.
timeline.why: Compare equivalent posterior lung sites, then percussion and tactile findings where the case supports them. Document the location of a focal abnormality.

timeline.action: Auscultate heart — aortic, pulmonic, tricuspid, mitral, on skin
timeline.finding: Regular tachycardia without murmur.
timeline.why: The course expects at least four listening posts, on skin.

timeline.action: Auscultate lungs — posterior, on skin, compare side to side, mouth open
timeline.finding: Focal inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right posterior base.
timeline.why: The course expects six posterior fields, mouth open, on skin, comparing sides.

timeline.action: Percuss lung fields — posterior, compare side to side
timeline.finding: Dullness over the right posterior base compared with the left.
timeline.why: This specific action releases only the finding shown here. Interpret it with the history; it does not confirm a diagnosis by itself.

timeline.action: Assess tactile fremitus — compare side to side
timeline.finding: Tactile fremitus is increased at the right posterior base.
timeline.why: This specific action releases only the finding shown here. Interpret it with the history; it does not confirm a diagnosis by itself.

timeline.action: Osteopathic structural screen — thoracic
timeline.finding: T1 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.
timeline.why: Name the level examined; findings are released by region.

timeline.action: Inspect skin — arms
timeline.finding: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
timeline.why: This specific action releases only the finding shown here. Interpret it with the history; it does not confirm a diagnosis by itself.

timeline.student: I recommend evaluating a lung infection, while checking how well you are breathing. The pattern can fit pneumonia, but an examination alone cannot prove the cause. We may need chest imaging and other tests before choosing treatment.
timeline.patient: Okay, that makes sense.
timeline.why: Proposed care, not a record of tests or treatment already completed.

timeline.student: What questions do you have about the next steps?
timeline.patient: Could I give this to the people at home?

timeline.student: Some causes of fever and cough can spread to people at home. Until the cause is clearer, cover coughs, clean your hands and limit close contact while you are ill. I recommend assessment of your breathing and a treatment plan based on the findings.
timeline.patient: Alright. Thank you for explaining that.
timeline.why: Answer the concern that was just expressed. Give a defensible recommendation and explain uncertainty; do not promise a diagnosis or recovery before the evidence supports it.

note.S:
cc: Fever, cough and pain on deep breathing

HPI: 25-year-old man with worsening productive cough; onset 4 days ago. Fever began the following day, measured 101.5 F at home. Yellow sputum, chills, fatigue and dyspnea on stairs. Nonradiating sharp right lower chest pain, 5/10, provoked by coughing/deep inspiration. Coworker had respiratory illness last week. Acetaminophen 500 mg twice yesterday lowered fever briefly. No previous similar episode.

Perspective: Could I give this to the people at home?

PMH: No chronic lung or heart disease; vaccines not reviewed recently.

PSH: Hernia repair at age 20.

Meds: Acetaminophen as above; no daily prescription medications.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Smokes 5 cigarettes daily for 5 years. Two alcoholic drinks weekly. No recreational drugs. Bus dispatcher; lives with wife; no recent travel, immobilization or surgery.

FH: My mother is fifty-two and she has asthma.; My father is fifty-five and he has high blood pressure.; I have one sister, she's twenty-seven and she's healthy.

ROS: Respiratory - Reports cough. Reports dyspnea. Denies hemoptysis. General - Reports fever. Reports chills. Reports fatigue. Cardiovascular - Reports chest pain. Denies edema. Denies syncope.
note.O:
Vitals: T 101.3 F oral, P 102 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg, R 22 rpm, Pulse Ox 95% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Tired appearing, alert and oriented, speaking full sentences.
Heart: Regular tachycardia without murmur.
Lungs: Focal inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right posterior base.
Lungs: Dullness over the right posterior base compared with the left.
Lungs: Tactile fremitus is increased at the right posterior base.
Osteopathic: T1 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.
Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Obtain chest x-ray and assess oxygenation, respiratory rate and severity to decide disposition; consider guideline-directed antibiotics after confirming the working diagnosis and allergy/comorbidity review; explain hydration and warning signs; reassess within 48–72 hours, sooner for worsening dyspnea, confusion or inability to drink.

2. Assess thromboembolic risk and use a validated diagnostic pathway if suspicion remains; obtain appropriate imaging rather than dismissing PE because fever is present; arrange urgent evaluation for clinical deterioration. If pulmonary embolism remains a concern, arrange emergency-department assessment; explain that fever does not rule out a clot and that increasing breathlessness or fainting requires immediate help.

3. Review smoking and persistent symptoms; ensure follow-up imaging or specialist evaluation if symptoms or consolidation do not resolve; offer smoking-cessation support and explain that cancer is a differential, not an established diagnosis.

reasoning.question: Are you breathless at rest, confused, or unable to drink?
reasoning.why: Severity and hydration determine disposition before a pathogen label does.
reasoning.if_present: These features require urgent assessment even if a respiratory infection seems likely.
reasoning.if_absent: If stable, examine focal lung findings and arrange appropriate testing and follow-up.
reasoning.next_action: Assess oxygenation, respiratory rate and posterior lung fields.
reasoning.document: Record the answer and findings only if obtained; keep possible diagnoses in Assessment and proposed investigations in Plan.

note.S:
cc: Fever, cough and pain on deep breathing

HPI: 25-year-old man with worsening productive cough; onset 7 days ago. Fever began the following day, measured 101.5 F at home. Yellow sputum, chills, fatigue and dyspnea on stairs. Nonradiating sharp right lower chest pain, 5/10, provoked by coughing/deep inspiration. Coworker had respiratory illness last week. Acetaminophen 500 mg twice yesterday lowered fever briefly. No previous similar episode.

Perspective: Could I give this to the people at home?

PMH: No chronic lung or heart disease; vaccines not reviewed recently.

PSH: Hernia repair at age 20.

Meds: Acetaminophen as above; no daily prescription medications.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Smokes 5 cigarettes daily for 5 years. Two alcoholic drinks weekly. No recreational drugs. Bus dispatcher; lives with wife; no recent travel, immobilization or surgery.

FH: My mother is fifty-two and she has asthma.; My father is fifty-five and he has high blood pressure.; I have one sister, she's twenty-seven and she's healthy.

ROS: Respiratory - Reports cough. Reports dyspnea. Denies hemoptysis. General - Reports fever. Reports chills. Reports fatigue. Cardiovascular - Reports chest pain. Denies edema. Denies syncope.
note.O:
Vitals: T 101.3 F oral, P 102 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg, R 22 rpm, Pulse Ox 95% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Tired appearing, alert and oriented, speaking full sentences.
Heart: Regular tachycardia without murmur.
Lungs: Focal inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right posterior base.
Lungs: Dullness over the right posterior base compared with the left.
Lungs: Tactile fremitus is increased at the right posterior base.
Osteopathic: T1 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.
Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Obtain chest x-ray and assess oxygenation, respiratory rate and severity to decide disposition; consider guideline-directed antibiotics after confirming the working diagnosis and allergy/comorbidity review; explain hydration and warning signs; reassess within 48–72 hours, sooner for worsening dyspnea, confusion or inability to drink.

2. Assess thromboembolic risk and use a validated diagnostic pathway if suspicion remains; obtain appropriate imaging rather than dismissing PE because fever is present; arrange urgent evaluation for clinical deterioration. If pulmonary embolism remains a concern, arrange emergency-department assessment; explain that fever does not rule out a clot and that increasing breathlessness or fainting requires immediate help.

3. Review smoking and persistent symptoms; ensure follow-up imaging or specialist evaluation if symptoms or consolidation do not resolve; offer smoking-cessation support and explain that cancer is a differential, not an established diagnosis.

note.S:
cc: Fever, cough and pain on deep breathing

HPI: 25-year-old man with worsening productive cough; onset 4 days ago. Fever began the following day, measured 101.5 F at home. Yellow sputum, chills, fatigue and dyspnea on stairs. Nonradiating sharp right lower chest pain, 5/10, provoked by coughing/deep inspiration. Coworker had respiratory illness last week. Acetaminophen 500 mg twice yesterday lowered fever briefly. No previous similar episode.

Perspective: Could I give this to the people at home?

PMH: No chronic lung or heart disease; vaccines not reviewed recently.

PSH: Hernia repair at age 20.

Meds: Acetaminophen as above; no daily prescription medications.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Smokes 5 cigarettes daily for 5 years. Two alcoholic drinks weekly. No recreational drugs. Bus dispatcher; lives with wife; no recent travel, immobilization or surgery.

FH: My mother is fifty-two and she has asthma.; My father is fifty-five and he has high blood pressure.; I have one sister, she's twenty-seven and she's healthy.

ROS: Respiratory - Reports cough. Reports dyspnea. Denies hemoptysis. General - Reports fever. Reports chills. Reports fatigue. Cardiovascular - Reports chest pain. Denies edema. Denies syncope.

Patient concern: I cannot read small print on medicine bottles without my glasses.
note.O:
Vitals: T 101.3 F oral, P 102 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg, R 22 rpm, Pulse Ox 95% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Tired appearing, alert and oriented, speaking full sentences.
Heart: Regular tachycardia without murmur.
Lungs: Focal inspiratory crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right posterior base.
Lungs: Dullness over the right posterior base compared with the left.
Lungs: Tactile fremitus is increased at the right posterior base.
Osteopathic: T1 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.
Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Obtain chest x-ray and assess oxygenation, respiratory rate and severity to decide disposition; consider guideline-directed antibiotics after confirming the working diagnosis and allergy/comorbidity review; explain hydration and warning signs; reassess within 48–72 hours, sooner for worsening dyspnea, confusion or inability to drink. Use large-print instructions and ask the patient to explain the medication and safety plan back.

2. Assess thromboembolic risk and use a validated diagnostic pathway if suspicion remains; obtain appropriate imaging rather than dismissing PE because fever is present; arrange urgent evaluation for clinical deterioration. If pulmonary embolism remains a concern, arrange emergency-department assessment; explain that fever does not rule out a clot and that increasing breathlessness or fainting requires immediate help.

3. Review smoking and persistent symptoms; ensure follow-up imaging or specialist evaluation if symptoms or consolidation do not resolve; offer smoking-cessation support and explain that cancer is a differential, not an established diagnosis.

reasoning.question: Are you breathless at rest, confused, or unable to drink?
reasoning.why: Severity and hydration determine disposition before a pathogen label does.
reasoning.if_present: These features require urgent assessment even if a respiratory infection seems likely.
reasoning.if_absent: If stable, examine focal lung findings and arrange appropriate testing and follow-up.
reasoning.next_action: Assess oxygenation, respiratory rate and posterior lung fields.
reasoning.document: Record the answer and findings only if obtained; keep possible diagnoses in Assessment and proposed investigations in Plan.

recall.prompt: Before naming a diagnosis, what is the key distinction in this presentation?
recall.answer: Clarify onset, sputum, breathlessness and pleuritic pain. Ask hemoptysis and thromboembolic risks rather than assuming every cough is infectious.

recall.prompt: Which specific examination or safety step changes what you can document?
recall.answer: Compare equivalent posterior lung sites, then percussion and tactile findings where the case supports them. Document the location of a focal abnormality.

recall.prompt: Name one tempting documentation or reasoning error and how you will prevent it.
recall.answer: Writing both lungs clear after listening at one site, or omitting oxygen saturation from the supplied vitals.
